text: 🇲🇽✊ "Something a ruler has to do is listen." — Presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum, Umán, Yucatán She is touring IMSS-Bienestar hospitals and health centers, and drops in on health centers unannounced — not even the governor or the mayor is told — because "when they say the president is coming, they fix everything, they paint it." She talks with patients and pharmacy staff, then meets hospital directors: "Total frankness." In Quintana Roo on Friday, the directors of all three hospitals told her they are better off with IMSS-Bienestar than before. Specialist appointments are up about 36% since 2024, and IMSS-Bienestar care is free.

🔥🇲🇽 "Do you know how much they owe now? Zero. They owe nothing." — Presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum, Umán, Yucatán She walked through three Yucatán cases. Julián Rodríguez borrowed 55,000 pesos for a home, had paid 218,000, and in 2024 owed one million. Miriam Elizabeth Chablé Arana borrowed 63,000, paid 380,000, owed 2,084,000. María Ortiz Chan borrowed 88,000, paid 277,000, owed one million. López Obrador froze Infonavit evictions and changed how loans were granted; her government restructured the old loans — more than 5 million of them.
banner: INFONAVIT DEBTS: FROM 1M PESOS TO ZERO

text: 🔥🇲🇽 "Infonavit was a loan-shark bank — no, you fell short, governor. They were thieves." — Octavio Romero Oropeza, director general of Infonavit, Umán, Yucatán Governor Joaquín Díaz Mena had thanked the president for changing Infonavit so it is "never again a loan-shark institution." Romero explained why: on top of interest and principal, Infonavit added the yearly minimum-wage increase to the balance, so debts rose even as people paid. 4,856,000 of these "unpayable" loans were restructured as of December 31 — 136,000 in Yucatán. Borrowers who finished paying but never released the mortgage lien, a procedure costing 16,000–18,000 pesos, now get it free: 84,000 families in Yucatán.

🇲🇽✊ "I'm already an older person, and today I have somewhere to live." — Teresa de Jesús García Ordóñez, 57, Infonavit home recipient, Umán, Yucatán She received one of the first 432 homes of the 5,360 being built at Punta Cruz Eco. Infonavit director Octavio Romero said low-wage housing used to mean 45 m² units far from cities, often without water, power or drainage; the president asked for 60 m² — two bedrooms, living-dining room, kitchen, full bathroom and service room — inside urban areas. Commercial value is about 1.2 million pesos; with permit and tax waivers from states and municipalities and Infonavit financing construction without interest, they sell at about half. Requirements: be an Infonavit member, earn 1 to 2.9 minimum wages, own no home — from age 18. Infonavit's Yucatán target is 60,000 homes; about 40,000 are contracted.

🇲🇽✊ "The governments of the past took from the people. And we give." — Presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum, Umán, Yucatán She spoke on October 17 at the handover of the first 432 of 5,360 homes at the Infonavit Punta Cruz Eco development in Umán, Yucatán. She closed: "For years there were governments that devoted themselves to governing for a few. Not us. We are the governments of the people, by the people and for the people of Mexico." She also told Umán that a campaign promise will be kept: a Rosario Castellanos university campus there, with medicine and nursing degrees.
banner: "THEY TOOK FROM THE PEOPLE. WE GIVE."

text:
🇲🇽🌎 <u>IMF: Mexico's Growth Holds at 2.1%, While Washington's T-MEC Reviews Are the Risk</u>

The IMF's Western Hemisphere department projects Mexico's economy growing 1.5% in 2026 and 1.8% in 2027, then holding at 2.1% a year from 2028 to 2031. US growth slows to 1.8% by 2031, and Canada stays at 1.7%. The risk it flags comes from the north. The annual T-MEC reviews that began in July "will likely generate greater uncertainty, shorten planning horizons, delay investment decisions," according to the report cited by El Financiero. A 10-point hike in regional or US content rules could cut Mexico's and Canada's long-run output by 0.5-1.0%, "with limited net impact for the United States."

🔥🇲🇽 <u>Morena Puts Querétaro's PAN on Notice as the 2027 Race Opens</u>

Querétaro's 2026-2027 local election process formally opened on October 16. Morena's representative at the state electoral institute (IEEQ), Itzi-Guari Hurtado Bañuelos, warned that the party will not tolerate public money, social programs or government structures being used to favor the ruling PAN's candidates. Social support belongs to the people, Morena said, and can't be used for electoral coercion. The party has already filed IEEQ complaints against PAN hopeful Luis Bernardo Nava, the former state social development secretary, for early campaigning and misuse of public resources, and over a billboard blitz promoting Querétaro City mayor Felifer Macías.
banner: QUERÉTARO: MORENA WARNS PAN ON STATE FUNDS

text:
🔥🇲🇽 <u>Mexico's Religious Right, From the Sinarquistas to CPAC</u>

In the final part of his Contralínea series, Pablo Moctezuma Barragán traces Mexico's religious right from the Unión Nacional Sinarquista, Los Tecos and MURO to today's faces: Eduardo Verástegui, who brought the Trump-linked CPAC to Mexico, the Frente Nacional por la Familia, Gilberto Lozano's anti-AMLO Frenaa, El Yunque and Red Familia. His conclusion: the US and Mexican religious right, Protestant and Catholic alike, "are today intimately united in the effort to further subordinate our country to the strategic interests of the United States."

🇲🇽🏘️ <u>Mexico City Expropriates a Roma Norte Lot to House the Otomí Families Living There</u>

Mexico City's government published a decree expropriating Avenida Chapultepec 380, in Roma Norte, for social housing. The 442-square-meter lot holds a vecindad rated a structural risk since 2016. The city's Housing Institute (INVI) will build a new apartment building for the Otomí community that lives there. Families move out during construction and return when it's finished, and INVI pays compensation to whoever proves legal ownership.
banner: ROMA NORTE LOT → OTOMÍ SOCIAL HOUSING

🚨🇲🇽 <u>Chihuahua's Former Prosecutor Arrested in the CIA Case</u>

César Jáuregui, Maru Campos's former state prosecutor, was arrested in Chihuahua on Saturday. A judge approved warrants on October 16 for him and for Guillermo Zuany, former head of the state's anti-kidnapping unit, on charges of unlawful exercise of public service and giving false statements to authorities. The case goes back to April 19, when a crash in the Chihuahua sierra killed two US agents later identified as CIA, along with two state investigators. The next day Jáuregui went on air to say only Mexican forces took part in the raid: about 40 soldiers and 40 state agents.
